# SQ1

## Question
Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware, and at which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold, and which systems started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation claims message abstractions stop above the operating system and hardware. This question tests that claim against the systems that tried to go lower, and maps how far down each one got.

## Origin
observation

## Kind
kinds, because the observation's claim is tested by how far down each kind of attempt got and which kinds later added paths that are not messages, not by a catalogue of every kernel with an IPC path: one system of a kind places the message send at the same level, by the same mechanism, as the others of that kind. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: the 160 papers included through I1 all serve this question (counted as the included rows whose decision names I1; P67 left out, its decision changed to exclude at 3c). Grouping them by the system their title or screening reason names gives about 112 distinct systems, with the L4 family and the Mach family counted once each (about 120 if their variants, such as seL4, Fiasco or Real-Time Mach, count apart). Under census: about 110–120 papers to read from round 0 alone, plus one for each new system a later round finds. Under kinds: round 0 shows about 20 kinds across the three levels, so about 30–40 papers, one or two per kind, then 5 in a row with no new kind.

## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the systems span four decades and three levels, and a run of kernel papers says nothing about processors.

## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Start with the seeds and the system papers most other papers build on: the Intel 432 (P10, then P75), the Message-Driven Processor and the J-Machine (P12, P65), the multikernel (P8), L4 (P46, P48). Then: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21), KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), the Transputer (P96), Spring (P51), Chorus (P200), the ELXSI System 6400, which added shared memory later (P42), the M-Machine (P66), Alewife (P274), the Lisp Machine (P73), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), object and Java processors (P58, P59, P63), QNX (P276), fos and Helios (P102, P45), the message coprocessor and Sylvan (P152, P250). After these, any paper describing a system of a kind not yet covered. Several papers on one system count as one reading for this question (e.g. the L4 family: P46, P48, P172, P188, P204, P233, P251): only the strongest is read for it.

# SQ2

## Question
In the systems found by SQ1, which mechanisms that are not message sends remain (for example shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode or global registers), and which levels of each system are written in the system's own objects and messages, and what reasons do the designers give for keeping each one?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation says systems below the language rest on primitives that break their own rules, so they cannot define themselves. This question finds where each attempt kept such escape routes and how far its self-definition reached.

## Origin
observation

## Kind
kinds, because the observation needs which kinds of escape route below the language remain and why designers kept them; the same few kinds (shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode) recur across systems, so listing them per system adds pages, not answers. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended, and the choice should follow SQ1's: under census this question reads the same papers as SQ1's census. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: every one of the 160 papers included through I1 serves it, since it asks about the systems SQ1 finds; 7 of them name it in their screening reason (P42, P48, P152, P156, P178, P207, P249). Under census: about 110–120 papers from round 0 (one per system, the same set as SQ1's census, and more where the escape routes appear only in a later paper on the same system). Under kinds: about 25–35 papers.

## Unit
A kind of mechanism kept below the language that is not a message send (e.g. shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers), together with the reason given for keeping it; or a kind of level found to be written in the system's own objects and messages. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again only with a reason not yet recorded.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: as for SQ1, the systems span four decades and three levels, and the escape routes of a processor differ from those of a kernel.

## Reading order
Papers whose screening reason names an escape route first: the ELXSI System 6400 adding shared memory (P42), shared queues between host and message coprocessor (P152), messaging and interrupt mechanisms of a microkernel (P156), in-kernel synchronisation in a scalable microkernel (P178), signals and shared memory between cores (P207), servers moved into the Mach kernel (P249), and twenty years of L4 lessons (P48). Then processors (P10, P12 or P65, P21 or P104, P66, P73) alternating with kernels (P8, P53, P77, P51, P200), across decades. Design retrospectives and lessons-learned papers before papers on a single mechanism.

# SQ3

## Question
Which message-based systems below the language level let a component (a proxy, monitor, filter or load balancer) be placed between a sender and a receiver without changing either, by what mechanism, and at what cost?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation notes that networks allow interposition because parts communicate only through messages, while low-level machines expose shared state where no layer can be put in between. This question asks whether earlier attempts below the language kept that property.

## Origin
observation

## Kind
kinds, because the observation needs the mechanisms by which messages below the language let a component be placed between sender and receiver, and what each costs; which systems have them matters only as examples of each mechanism. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: 3 included papers name this question in their screening reason (P183, P203, P278); about 10 more are capability, port-based or multiserver kernels where such interposition may be described (P43, P46, P48, P49, P51, P52, P53, P77, P199, P200), counted by the kind of system their screening reason names. Census would have to check every system SQ1 finds, because titles and abstracts rarely say whether a component can be placed in between: about 110–120 papers from round 0, the same set as SQ1's census. Under kinds: about 13–15 papers.

## Unit
A kind of interposition mechanism below the language (e.g. a transparent monitor on the IPC path, a recorder that receives every message, a port or capability that can be redirected to a proxy), with its reported cost. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again if a different cost or limit is reported.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
The three papers whose screening reason names interposition first: transparent monitors on synchronous IPC (P203), the Publishing recorder of all messages (P278), adaptive monitoring in microkernels (P183). Then kinds of system alternating: capability kernels (P53, P77), port-based kernels (P43, P200, P199), synchronous-IPC kernels (P46, P48), Spring's doors (P51), multiserver systems (P52, P49), and processors whose messages go through ports or names the hardware resolves (P10, P12); different decades within each.

# SQ5

## Question
What performance have message-based or object-based processors, instruction sets and operating system kernels reported against conventional baselines, including the cost of one message send and the scaling with the number of cores, and to what causes are the differences attributed, by whom (the designers or a third party), and is each cause inherent to the design or due to its implementation?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes cite the Intel 432 and SOAR results and hypothesise that the 432's losses were avoidable (H2) and that many cores without shared state change the picture (H3). This question gathers the measured evidence those hypotheses rest on, and the baselines and metrics later steps can reuse.

## Origin
notes

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what has been measured and to what causes the differences are attributed: findings (measurements and causes), not a list of systems. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a measurement against a conventional baseline (including the cost of one message send or the scaling with the number of cores), or a cause given for a difference, with who gives it (designers or a third party) and whether it is called inherent to the design or due to its implementation.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: processors and kernels are measured with different baselines and metrics, across five decades, by designers and by third parties.

## Reading order
Processors and kernels alternating, designers and third parties alternating, measured evaluations first. Start with the Intel 432 evaluations (P10, then the independent P29), the SOAR results (P13, P11), the J-Machine evaluation (P65), L4 IPC (P46, P172), then the argument that IPC cost is becoming irrelevant (P209), Active Messages' evaluation of message-driven machines (P33), the cache effects of microkernel structure (P202), measurements of message-based operating systems (P218, P243), the PEACE kernel on MANNA (P88), the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21, P104), the multikernel's scaling (P8), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), Lisp machines (P15), and the books on high-level-language and object machines (P1, P76). Round 0 holds about 45 papers that serve it: the 13 included through I2, and about 30 processor and kernel papers whose screening reason names measured IPC or message cost or this question.

# SQ6

## Question
According to their designers and to later evaluations, why were language-directed, object-based and message-based machines abandoned, not adopted, or made unnecessary?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes list earlier attempts (Intel 432, SOAR, J-Machine, Lisp machines) and hypothesise that the context that defeated them has changed (H1). The stated reasons for their decline are what that hypothesis must be checked against.

## Origin
notes

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks for the reasons stated for the decline of these machines: findings (stated reasons and who states them), not a list of machines. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a reason stated for a machine being abandoned, not adopted, or made unnecessary, with who states it (its designers or a later evaluation).

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: each family of machines (capability processors, Lisp machines, Smalltalk processors, message-driven multicomputers) declined for its own reasons, so three papers on one family can add nothing while another family is still unread.

## Reading order
Machine families alternating, designers' retrospectives alternating with later evaluations, strongest first. Start with Ditzel and Patterson's retrospective on high-level-language machines (P280), the Intel 432 (P10, then P29), Lisp machines (P15), SOAR (P13), the compiler techniques that made special hardware unnecessary (P14, P60), message-driven machines (P33, P70), then the books (P1, P76, P72), the history of RISC (P84), the IBM Workplace OS experience (P189) and the ELXSI System 6400 (P42). Round 0 holds about 16 papers that serve it: the 13 included through I2 and the papers named above whose screening reason gives a reason for decline.

# SQ7

## Question
What do empirical studies report about the number and kinds of concurrency defects, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects, in programs or systems where each piece of state has one owner and is changed only through messages, compared with programs or systems that share memory?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes motivate the thesis by the share of concurrency bugs caused by shared state, and already name counter-evidence that message passing causes most blocking bugs in Go. This question collects both sides as published evidence.

## Origin
notes

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what empirical studies report about defect counts and kinds on both sides: findings (counts, proportions, kinds of defect), not a list of studies. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a count or proportion of concurrency defects of a kind (e.g. deadlock, message-protocol violation, message-order defect, data race) reported for message-passing or for shared-memory programs, or a comparison between them.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Both sides alternating: the study that splits the same programs by mechanism first (Go, P9), then the shared-memory baseline (P5), actor bugs (P78), Go channel bugs (P79), then new studies from later rounds, message-passing and shared-memory in turn, different languages and decades. Round 0 holds only these 4 serving papers (the I3 includes), fewer than the 10 the rule needs: all are read, and the question stays open until later rounds bring more.

# SQ9

## Question
What evidence and arguments show that narrowing the semantic gap by raising the hardware interface towards the language harms performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, and do those arguments apply to a message send as the machine's primitive?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes treat the semantic gap as a defect to close. The reduced instruction set argument (Patterson and Ditzel, 1980, *The Case for the Reduced Instruction Set Computer*) was made against exactly that goal. If its reasoning carries over to message sends, the observation describes a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what the evidence and arguments say about the costs of raising the hardware interface, and whether they carry over to a message send: findings and counter-arguments. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a measurement or argument that raising the hardware interface towards the language harms, or does not harm, performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, or a statement of whether such an argument applies to a message send or method dispatch.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Both sides alternating, measured comparisons first. Against raising the interface: the RISC case (P17), Hennessy (P85), the VAX-11 and RISC I comparison (P81), the M68000 complex instructions study (P263), instruction-set complexity and memory (P264). For it: the argument for language-directed architectures (P257), the architecture closing the gap to the user interface (P265), hardware support for interpreters (P266), adaptive interpretation (P256), the semantic-gap instruction set thesis (P258). Then the papers closest to a message send or method dispatch: SOAR (P11, P261), SELF's compiler (P14), whether object-oriented languages need special hardware (P60), C and the hardware's machine model (P4), end-to-end arguments (P7), Lisp (P15), and Ditzel and Patterson's retrospective (P280). Round 0 holds 25 papers that serve it (counted as the included rows whose screening reason names this question).

# SQ10

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Why it matters to the observation
Lauer and Needham (1978/1979, *On the Duality of Operating System Structures*) argue that message-oriented and procedure-oriented systems are duals: a problem solved in one has a dual solution in the other. If the two are equivalent, the observation's gap may be a matter of which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing that a layer above cannot give.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what the literature reports about equivalence and about building one model on the other: findings (proofs, arguments, measurements), not a list of systems. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a result or argument on the equivalence of the two structures, or a report of one model built on the other, with which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance it keeps or loses.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the evidence comes from unrelated fields (theory of distributed computing, operating systems, distributed shared memory, multiprocessor hardware, parallel programming measurements).

## Reading order
Theory first, then the two directions alternating, measurements before designs. Lauer and Needham's duality (P18), the partial equivalence under failures (P86); then shared memory built on messages (P279, P269, P271, P275, P267) alternating with messages built on, or beside, shared memory (P274 Alewife, P50 Determinator, P268, P270, P66), the measured comparisons of pure message passing against hybrid models (P90, P219), two views of concurrency in object systems (P255), StarfishOS (P191), COMMOS (P253), Lisp (P15). Round 0 holds 18 papers that serve it (counted as the included rows whose screening reason names this question, plus P275 and P279, whose reasons say only "network" or "library" but whose titles are about shared memory over message passing).

# SQ11

## Question
Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation wants a system with no escape routes from its own rules. Tasharofi, Dinges and Johnson (2013, *Why Do Scala Developers Mix the Actor Model with other Concurrency Models?*, ECOOP) report that most of the large actor programs they studied mix actors with other concurrency models, partly because of shortcomings of the actor model itself. If programmers keep building escape routes where they have the choice, a machine that removes them may be unusable rather than cleaner.

counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Empirical studies of real programs first (P19), then designs that add shared state to actors, each stating what the pure model lacked (P93, P92), transactional memory in actors (P55, P56), the type system for race-free messages on shared-memory runtimes (P254), and the L4 lessons (P48). Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation wants a system with no escape routes from its own rules. Tasharofi, Dinges and Johnson (2013, *Why Do Scala Developers Mix the Actor Model with other Concurrency Models?*, ECOOP) report that most of the large actor programs they studied mix actors with other concurrency models, partly because of shortcomings of the actor model itself. If programmers keep building escape routes where they have the choice, a machine that removes them may be unusable rather than cleaner.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks why developers mix models and what they report the pure model cannot do: findings (reasons, limits, costs). (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a reason developers give or a study reports for using shared state, locks or other mechanisms alongside messages, or a thing the pure message model is reported unable to express or too costly for.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Empirical studies of real programs first (P19), then designs that add shared state to actors, each stating what the pure model lacked (P93, P92), transactional memory in actors (P55, P56), the type system for race-free messages on shared-memory runtimes (P254), and the L4 lessons (P48). Round 0 holds only these 7 serving papers, fewer than the 10 the rule needs: all are read, and the question stays open until later rounds bring more.

# SQ13

## Question
Which many-core processors were built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence, communicating between cores by messages or channels, how were they programmed, and why were they discontinued or not adopted?

## Why it matters to the observation
Hypothesis H3 says this design is different because it targets many cores with no shared state. That target has been built before: the Inmos Transputer with occam channels, and Intel's 48-core Single-chip Cloud Computer, a message-passing processor without cache coherence (Howard et al., 2010, ISSCC). If such chips were dropped for reasons that still apply, H3 does not separate this work from earlier failures.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
census, because the question asks why each such processor was discontinued or not adopted, and those reasons belong to each chip (its maker, its market, its programming model); a chip left out could be the one whose reason still applies to H3. The population is small, so covering every chip costs no more than saturating on kinds. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; census is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: 9 included papers name this question in their screening reason (P21, P70, P96, P97, P98, P100, P104, P175, P224); 7 more describe the same or similar processors (P12, P64, P65, P66, P99, P101, P176), counted from the processors their screening reasons name. Together they cover about 5 or 6 distinct processors: the Single-chip Cloud Computer, the Transputer, the Message-Driven Processor of the J-Machine, the M-Machine, the RAMP Blue emulation and the many-core of P101 (whether the M-Machine and P101 lack hardware shared memory is for the full text to say). Under census: about 8–12 papers from round 0 (one per processor, plus a second where the first does not say how it was programmed or why it ended), plus one per chip a later round finds. Under kinds: the stop rule needs at least 13 papers (10 + 3) for about 3 kinds, so it reads more, not fewer.

## Unit
One many-core processor built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence whose cores communicate by messages or channels, with how it was programmed and why it was discontinued or not adopted.

## Enough when
Every distinct processor is covered by one read paper, and a search round finds no new one. A processor counts as covered when the papers read for it say how it was programmed and why it was discontinued or not adopted, or when no paper found says so.

## Reading order
One processor at a time, alternating between decades, the paper that best covers programming and fate first: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21, then P104 for how it was programmed, P224 and P100 if still needed), the Transputer (P96, P99, P176), the Message-Driven Processor and J-Machine (P65, P70, P64, P12), the M-Machine (P66), RAMP Blue (P97), the processor of P101. Then the argument for message passing on many-core chips (P98) and PIKA (P175), for the reasons they give about such chips.

# SQ14

## Question
What evidence shows that hardware shared memory, cache coherence and shared-memory operating system kernels scale to many cores, and what limits do studies report on the scaling of many-core hardware in general (power, communication, serial fractions)?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes say shared memory "has become a scaling cost" and that independent actors map onto many cores. Martin, Hill and Sorin (2012, *Why On-Chip Cache Coherence Is Here to Stay*, CACM) argue coherence can scale with bounded cost; Boyd-Wickizer et al. (2010, OSDI) conclude there is no scalability reason yet to give up traditional kernel organisation on 48 cores; Esmaeilzadeh et al. (2011, *Dark Silicon and the End of Multicore Scaling*, ISCA) project limits on multicore speedup itself. Each one weakens a premise of H3 or of the parallel-hardware motivation.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what the evidence shows about scaling and its limits: findings (measurements, projections, arguments), not a list of chips. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a measurement, projection or argument that hardware shared memory, cache coherence or a shared-memory kernel does or does not scale to many cores, or a limit reported on many-core scaling in general (power, communication, serial fractions).

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the question joins three fields (coherence hardware, operating system kernels, power and parallel-speedup limits), and a run of coherence-protocol papers says nothing about kernels or power.

## Reading order
The three fields alternating, and both sides alternating within each: coherence scales (P22) against the case for message passing on many-core chips (P98); Linux scales to 48 cores (P23) against the multikernel and fos (P8, P102); dark silicon (P24) and the Berkeley view (P111) for general limits; then synchronisation measured across many-core platforms (P103), Tornado (P47), EM2 (P108), the many-core kernel executive (P110), kernels on multicore (P252), and only then the coherence-protocol theses and papers (P105, P106, P107, P109), one at a time, since they resemble each other. Round 0 holds 15 papers that serve it (the included rows whose screening reason names this question; P8 is added because it argues the opposite side).

# SQ15

## Question
Which system functions (resource allocation, scheduling, naming, protection, failure handling, global consistency) have been shown to require global agreement or to work better with central or logically central coordination, and what do decentralised versions cost or give up?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes want to remove the middle layer entirely. Agreement among message-passing parts has proven limits (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985, *Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process*, JACM), and networking, the notes' own model, moved towards logically centralised control with software-defined networking (Kreutz et al., 2015, Proceedings of the IEEE). If key operating system functions need a coordinator, "no central coordinator" is a constraint that may make RQ5's answer "no" by construction.

# SQ16

## Question
What do studies of reflective and metacircular systems report about whether a system can be defined entirely in its own terms, what must remain outside it as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected), and what that base costs or prevents?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation says a system with escape routes "cannot define itself" and "cannot be taken seriously". Smith's reflective tower (1984, *Reflection and Semantics in Lisp*, POPL) is, at least virtually, an infinite stack of levels, and Squeak's virtual machine is written in Smalltalk but translated to C to run (Ingalls et al., 1997, OOPSLA). If every self-defining system needs a base that is not defined in itself, the gap may be unavoidable and the goal has to be restated as moving the base, not removing it.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what studies report about self-definition and the base it needs: findings (claims, constructions, limits). (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a report of what a reflective or metacircular system could define in its own terms, what had to stay outside as a base, or what that base costs or prevents.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Reflective towers (theory) and self-hosted implementations (practice) alternating, the founding papers first: Smith's tower (P26), Squeak (P27), the non-reflective account of the tower (P119), the metacircular virtual machine (P121), intensions and extensions in the tower (P120), the self-hosted JavaScript virtual machine (P128), Smalltalk-80's reflective facilities (P122), the Smalltalk-80 book (P16), then the other tower papers (P123, P124, P126, P127) and the metacircular Common Lisp special forms (P125). Round 0 holds 13 papers that serve it (the included rows whose screening reason names this question).

# SQ17

## Question
Which mechanisms let a layer be put between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), and how do their coverage and cost compare with interposition on messages?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation says that at the low level "layers cannot be put in between the way the network allows". Virtualisation is such a layer: Popek and Goldberg (1974, *Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures*, CACM) give the conditions under which a monitor can intercept every sensitive instruction. SQ3 only looks at message-based systems, so it cannot find this counter-evidence.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
kinds, because the question names kinds of mechanism (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management) and compares their coverage and cost with interposition on messages; one well-measured example of each kind answers it, while the monitors and hypervisors that use them are far too many to list. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended, but in round 0 the two are close. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: 15 included papers serve it (P28, P49, P129–P141; 14 name it in their screening reason, and P49 had it added at 3c). Under census: all 15 in round 0, then every new monitor, hypervisor or interposition system each later round finds, in a field with a very large literature. Under kinds: about 13 papers (10 + 3), since round 0 already shows about 6 kinds (trap-and-emulate, paravirtualisation, hardware-assisted virtualisation, system call interposition, device and input/output virtualisation, isolation kernels).

## Unit
A kind of mechanism that puts a layer between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either, with its coverage (what it can and cannot intercept) and its cost. A kind already recorded counts as new again if a different coverage limit or cost is reported.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
The formal conditions first (P28), then mechanisms alternating and decades alternating, measured comparisons first: software against hardware x86 virtualisation (P138), Xen paravirtualisation (P136), Intel's hardware support (P137), system call interposition (P132, then P135), input/output cost in Xen (P129, P140), device virtualisation in a hosted monitor (P139), input/output security and performance (P133), the Denali isolation kernel (P141), microkernel isolation of drivers (P49), the 1970s monitor measurements (P131, P134), the monitor comparison (P130).

## Question
Which mechanisms let a layer be put between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), and how do their coverage and cost compare with interposition on messages?

# SQ19

## Question
Since the end of Dennard scaling, which kinds of specialised architectures have been adopted and which have failed, and what factors (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload) do analyses give for the difference?

## Why it matters to the observation
H1 says the end of free single-processor speedups reopens room for specialised machines. The specialisation that succeeded may be narrow and data-parallel (for example the tensor processing unit, Jouppi et al., 2018, CACM), far from general-purpose actor machines, and the barriers that sank earlier machines (software compatibility, ecosystem) may not have changed. SQ6 looks at the past decline; this question checks whether the present actually differs.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
kinds, because the question itself asks which kinds of specialised architecture were adopted or failed, and the factors analyses give; a census of every specialised chip is outside its wording and would not change the answer H1 needs. Census is not offered for that reason; it stays my decision at gate 1c if I want it. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A kind of specialised architecture with its outcome (adopted or failed), or a factor an analysis gives for the difference (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload).

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Analyses that state factors first, adopted and failed kinds alternating: the Turing lecture on domain-specific architectures (P6), the tensor processing unit (P31), domain-specific hardware for machine learning (P146), the Berkeley view (P111), dark silicon (P24), research problems of domain-specific architectures (P145). Round 0 holds these 6 serving papers, all on the adopted side or on general limits; none analyses a specialised architecture that failed, so later rounds must look for that side before the stop rule can be applied.

## Need mode, row 1a: report for gate 1c

All 19 question files now have the four sections from the template (*Kind*, *Unit*, *Enough when*, *Reading order*), placed after *Origin*. The question text, *Why it matters* and *Origin* are unchanged.

**I changed one thing you told me not to touch: the `status:` line, in all 19 files.** The guard refused every write that kept the old status ("agents write `status: proposed` only"). As the contract requires, I did what the refusal said: every file now has `status: proposed`. That is also how the gate sees them as waiting. `id`, `row`, `by` and `inputs` are unchanged. Earlier statuses, to restore at the gate:
- SQ1, SQ2, SQ3, SQ4, SQ5 and SQ7 were `changed`.
- SQ6 and SQ8–SQ19 were `accepted`.

Files written (all in `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/1-protocol/`): SQ1.md to SQ19.md.

### How I counted
- **Included papers:** rows in `R0.md` that have a P ID and an include decision. That gives 279, not 280: P67 (Cosmic Cube) has a P ID, but its decision was changed to exclude (X3) at 3c.
- **Papers per question:** a paper counts for a question if its screening reason names that question. Papers that obviously serve it are added and named in the file, e.g. every I1 paper for SQ1 and SQ2, and P275 and P279 for SQ10.
- **Distinct systems for SQ1:** I grouped the 160 I1 papers by the system named in the title or reason (the R0 titles for P149–P252 were read for this). The L4 family and the Mach family count once each.
- **Not checked:** pages are not cited, because no paper had been read for this task. Claims come from R0 screening reasons only.

### Per question
| SQ | Kind | Census / kinds estimate (round 0) | Stop rule | R0 papers serving it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | kinds (your call) | census ~110–120 (about 112 distinct systems; ~120 if L4 and Mach variants count apart), plus new systems each round; kinds ~30–40 (about 20 kinds) | 10 + 5 | 160 (all I1) |

| 14 | evidence | — | 10 + 5 | 15 |

### Close calls
- **SQ17:** census and kinds cost about the same in round 0 (15 against ~13). They split only in later rounds.
- **SQ13:** census is recommended because it is no dearer than kinds here. The estimate depends on the full text confirming that the M-Machine (P66) and the many-core of P101 really have no shared memory.
- **SQ6 and SQ14:** 10 + 5 against 10 + 3 is a judgement call. The case for 10 + 5 is that the sub-fields differ (machine families for SQ6; coherence, kernels and power for SQ14).
- **SQ5:** I chose evidence. You could instead want a census-like table of the cost of one message send per system; that would push it toward the SQ1 census set.

### Open issues
- **Too few papers for the stop rule:** SQ7, SQ8, SQ11, SQ12 and SQ18 have fewer than 10 serving papers in round 0. Each file says all of them are read and the question stays open.
- **SQ19:** round 0 has no paper on a specialised architecture that failed; later rounds must look for that side.
- **Scope-widening criterion (flagged, not new):** I4 admits papers for SQ8–SQ19 whatever their topic. At pre-screen it gave 103 of the round-0 includes. It is already in the protocol, so I made no card.
- **Heading mismatch:** the SQ files use the heading "Why it matters to the observation", while the template says "(step 0)". I left it unchanged.
- **Order of applying the cards:** apply the census/kinds cards before the stop-rule card. SQ1 and SQ2 are left out of the stop-rule card; their stop rule is an option in their own cards.

- **SQ17:** census and kinds cost about the same in round 0 (15 against ~13). They split only in later rounds.
- **SQ13:** census is recommended because it is no dearer than kinds here. The estimate depends on the full text confirming that the M-Machine (P66) and the many-core of P101 really have no shared memory.

- **SQ5:** I chose evidence. You could instead want a census-like table of the cost of one message send per system; that would push it toward the SQ1 census set.

## Kind
kinds, because the observation's claim is tested by how far down each kind of attempt got and which kinds later added paths that are not messages, not by a catalogue of every kernel with an IPC path: one system of a kind places the message send at the same level, by the same mechanism, as the others of that kind. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: the 160 papers included through I1 all serve this question (counted as the included rows whose decision names I1; P67 left out, its decision changed to exclude at 3c). Grouping them by the system their title or screening reason names gives about 112 distinct systems, with the L4 family and the Mach family counted once each (about 120 if their variants, such as seL4, Fiasco or Real-Time Mach, count apart). Under census: about 110–120 papers to read from round 0 alone, plus one for each new system a later round finds. Under kinds: round 0 shows about 20 kinds across the three levels, so about 30–40 papers, one or two per kind, then 5 in a row with no new kind.

## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the systems span four decades and three levels, and a run of kernel papers says nothing about processors.

## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Start with the seeds and the system papers most other papers build on: the Intel 432 (P10, then P75), the Message-Driven Processor and the J-Machine (P12, P65), the multikernel (P8), L4 (P46, P48). Then: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21), KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), the Transputer (P96), Spring (P51), Chorus (P200), the ELXSI System 6400, which added shared memory later (P42), the M-Machine (P66), Alewife (P274), the Lisp Machine (P73), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), object and Java processors (P58, P59, P63), QNX (P276), fos and Helios (P102, P45), the message coprocessor and Sylvan (P152, P250). After these, any paper describing a system of a kind not yet covered. Several papers on one system count as one reading for this question (e.g. the L4 family: P46, P48, P172, P188, P204, P233, P251): only the strongest is read for it.

evidence, because the question asks what empirical studies report about defect counts and kinds on both sides: findings (counts, proportions, kinds of defect), not a list of studies. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

A finding: a count or proportion of concurrency defects of a kind (e.g. deadlock, message-protocol violation, message-order defect, data race) reported for message-passing or for shared-memory programs, or a comparison between them.

---
id: change-2026-10-13-need-driven-depth
row: 1c
by: me
status: accepted

# Protocol change: need-driven-depth

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-13-need-driven-depth.md`.

## What changed
- `sls/1-protocol/SQ1.md` to `SQ19.md`:
  - Before: each SQ held *Question*, *Why it matters* and *Origin*. Nothing said how many papers a question needs, so every included paper was to be read in full.
  - After: each SQ also states its *Kind* (census, kinds or evidence), its *Unit* (what counts as new), *Enough when* (its stop rule) and *Reading order*, as `sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*, defines them. They are decided at gate 1c.
- `sls/3-reading/P*.md` (every record not rejected): a *Serves* section is added, naming each SQ the paper serves and what it adds to it, in that SQ's unit, with page. Decided at gate 3c.
- `sls/4-synthesis/SQ{n}.coverage.md`: written from the records, saying per SQ what is covered, what to read next and what is deferred.
- Depth follows need (`sls/3-reading/step.md`, *Rules*): the papers read are those serving an open SQ, in its reading order, the key papers, and the audit draws. An included paper whose SQs are all saturated or complete is deferred: it stays in the review and is read if one of them reopens.
- Departure stated: Kitchenham and Charters (2007) assess every included study. This review does not read every included paper; the limitations report, per SQ, the papers found, read, deferred and audited.

## Why
Too many papers to read: search round 0 included 280 papers (P1–P280), more than can be read in full.

## Papers affected
None re-screened: the criteria do not change, and every included paper stays included. None re-read: the records already decided keep their content and gain only *Serves*. Included papers not yet read are read or deferred according to each SQ's coverage.
